characters: Mawunyo: a 14-year-old girl with shoulder-length braids in a maroon JHS uniform, carrying an exercise book.
Bright: Mawunyo’s classmate, 14, in the same uniform, outgoing and quick with ideas.
The wholesale trader: a middle-aged man at a market stall of phone accessories, in a striped shirt.
The customer: a girl from JHS 1, who asks if a case is strong.

narrationPlan.voice: Clear, conversational voice that slows down for calculations
narrationPlan.pace: Steady, reading numbers and sums slowly (about 130 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light upbeat marimba with a soft pulse (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Phone accessories and small trading are familiar in Ghanaian towns; Mawunyo is a verified Ewe name meaning "God is good". This is a supervised school enterprise with parent help, not a story about children leaving school to work.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Prices are invented and should be localised.

teacherGuide.overview: A short enterprise story that counts real costs and measures success in more than cedis. It is framed as a supervised school project and does not suggest that children should miss school to trade.
learningGoals: Calculate cost, income and profit with units.
Explain why the cost of getting goods to market is part of the true cost.
Explain how honest communication builds trust.
beforeReading: Ask: what does “profit” mean and what costs might a small trader forget?
whileReading: At pages 3, 4 and 7, ask learners to work out the sums before the text does.
afterReading: Plan a pretend (not real) enterprise with a survey, cost sheet and price list.
discussion: Why was 330 cedis the true cost?
What are the benefits and risks of lowering the price on the last seven cases?
reflection: What would count as success for you apart from profit?

mathsExtension.task: Work out the total cost: 25 cases at 12 cedis each plus a 30-cedi fare.
What is the profit on the first 18 cases?
Total profit after selling the last 7 at 15 cedis?
After giving 15 cedis to the library box, how much does each friend receive?

support: Provide a template table for cost, income and profit.
stretch: What price per case would give a profit of at least 150 cedis if all 25 sold at the same price? (Answer: more than 480 ÷ 25 = 19.2, so 20 cedis would give 25 × 20 − 330 = 170 cedis.)

culturalNotes: Phone accessories and small trading are familiar in Ghanaian towns; Mawunyo is a verified Ewe name meaning "God is good". This is a supervised school enterprise with parent help, not a story about children leaving school to work.
localiseThis: Replace the prices with realistic local figures.
Check school rules about selling at school.
Make sure any real project is supervised by an adult and does not disrupt learning or involve unsafe travel.
